items.title: “What joy to return to Chiclayo”: Leo XIV celebrates Mass in his former diocese
items.summary:
“What joy to return to Chiclayo.” With those words, Pope Leo XIV opened his homily on November 13, his first public address since returning to the diocese where he served as bishop for nine years, from 2014 to 2023. “It is a blessing for me to be among you again,” he continued, making no effort to conceal his emotion, and assuring the faithful that he had kept them in his prayers. After a warm welcome at Chiclayo’s air base earlier that morning, Leo immediately made his way to the vast plain of Pampas de Pimentel, a broad sandy expanse a few kilometers outside the city. Before entering the sacristy, he completed a full circuit in the popemobile among the 500,000 people gathered there, according to local authorities, in an atmosphere of euphoria that persisted despite oppressive heat and the dust that hung over the dry terrain. The crowd included Chiclayo residents who had known Bishop Read More…

items.title: As Leo XIV returns to Chiclayo, the city comes out to meet him
items.summary:
Leo XIV landed at the Teniente Coronel Pedro Ruiz Gallo airport shortly after 9 a.m., stepping off a LATAM Airlines A320 that had departed Lima’s Callao military base at dawn. What waited for him was, yet again, a homecoming: folk dancers in traditional dress waving white handkerchiefs, flags of Peru and the Vatican crossing in choreographed patterns, and former colleagues from the diocese waiting on the tarmac to embrace him. An estimated one million people lined the 14 kilometers of road between the airport and the Pampas de Pimentel esplanade, where the Mass was scheduled. The scenes echoed Lima two days earlier: hands extended toward the popemobile, streets thick with people who had traveled from across the region of Lambayeque to see the man who had been their bishop from 2015 to 2023. “Today, our father, our brother, and our friend returns home, to his land,” said Sister Karina, a religious of the diocese, told Read More…

items.title: Leo XIV and young people: What this South American tour is building
items.summary:
Something has been visible throughout Pope Leo XIV’s ongoing journey through Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru: the man is genuinely at ease with young people. Three countries, three youth vigils, and crowds that, taken together, number well over a million. In Montevideo, some 100,000 gathered at the Estadio Centenario on November 7 for a prayer vigil that seemed to set the tone for everything that followed. items.title: Why Pope Leo’s blue chasuble is one of the rarest vestments
items.summary:
While celebrating Mass in front of the Basilica of Our Lady of Lujan in Buenos Aires, Argentina, Pope Leo wore a striking sky-blue chasuble. The image of Our Lady of Lujan has that same color. It was a rare occurrence, as generally speaking, blue is not a liturgical color that can be worn at Mass. Officially priests can wear vestments that are primarily white (or gold), red, green, violet (or rose) and, in some cases, black. These vestments can have various trim colors, such as blue, but the vestment must be primarily one of the above colors. Yet, popes have given particular regions of the world the permission to wear blue vestments. Historically speaking Catholics in Spain (including many Spanish kings) were pivotal in promoting devotion to the Marian dogma of the Immaculate Conception. items.title: After his emotional return, Pope denounces ‘machismo’ in Peru and demands women be protected
items.summary:
LIMA, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV on Thursday denounced widespread “machismo” and violence against women in Peru, demanding that women be protected and respected as he set out marching orders for his beloved Peruvian church and people. 

After his emotional homecoming Wednesday, the Peruvian pope got down to business and turned to the challenges facing a church and country he knows well.

He called on the influential Catholic hierarchy to be models of unity and communion, and instructed Peruvian bishops to accompany their flocks and respond to victims of clergy sexual abuse with truth and justice.

But the 71-year-old pope also showed himself to be positively overjoyed to be home and as relaxed as he has been in public since his 2025 election.

Leo sang along enthusiastically as 40,000 people in Lima’s Plaza Mayor serenaded him with “Contigo Perú,” a famous song from Peru’s Pacific coast that celebrates national unity. He drew huge applause when he recited the lyrics of another famous Creole hymn, “Mi Perú.”

“It’s a blessing not only for us Chiclayans but for all of Peru,” said Ángel Esquives, a craftsman originally from Leo’s former diocese in Chiclayo who now lives in Lima. He said he left his home at 3 a.m. to go to the historic center and stand in line to get as close as possible to the pope.

items.title: German ambassador to Vatican says Pope Leo XIV wants to visit Germany
items.summary:
According to Germany’s ambassador to the Vatican, Pope Leo XIV intends to visit the central European country.

Bruno Kahl, 63, said to Colonge-based Catholic website, domradio.de , that it was too early to start planning the trip but Leo’s intentions were clear.

“On behalf of the Federal Government, I renewed the invitation previously extended by the Federal President and confirmed by the Federal Foreign Minister. The answer is already clear: he intends to come to Germany,” he said. 

“However, the exact sequence of his upcoming trips is not yet fully defined. He himself says he advised his predecessor to visit Germany and will, of course, heed that advice. It is still too early for concrete planning, though,” he added.

Crux Now ‘s request for comment from the Vatican press office was without immediate reply.

Kahl also said his impressions of the pope were very positive.

“I was very impressed,” Kahl said. “The Pope is approachable, open, straightforward, speaks in an uncomplicated, direct way, and makes you feel personally taken seriously,” he said. 

“He is very quick-witted, humorous, and therefore an exceptionally pleasant conversationalist,” he also said.

Kahl had previously been critical of the Vatican’s stance on the war between Russia and Ukraine, particularly during Pope Francis’ pontificate, but he was more approving of Leo’s view on the conflict.

“First, I need to correct that somewhat,” he said when asked about his previous comments. 

“Especially regarding the criticism of equidistance, there has been progress between the pontificate of Francis and that…

items.title: Pontifex Maximus, the plane renamed for Leo XIV
items.summary:
A small detail on the papal plane caught the attention and curiosity of those who followed the live broadcasts of the many flights Leo XIV took during his visit to Argentina: on the fuselage of the plane, the words “Pontifex Maximus” can be read. This is an ancient Latin expression meaning “supreme pontiff” or “highest pontiff.” Its roots, however, run far deeper than the Church. The word pontifex is a compound of two Latin roots: pons (bridge) and facio (to make). A pontifex, literally, is a bridge-builder. Scholars have long debated whether this was originally meant in a physical sense — pagan Roman priests who supervised or consecrated the sacred bridges over the Tiber, which carried enormous religious significance in early Rome — or whether it was always a metaphor for one who mediates between the human and the divine. The question remains open, but the image endured: the pope as the one who maintains Read More…

items.title: ‘Christianophobia’ added to dictionary by Royal Spanish Academy
items.summary:
Spain’s royal language watchdog has officially added “Christianophobia” to its dictionary.

The Royal Spanish Academy (RAE) has added the term “Christianophobia” to the 24th edition of its official book of words in the Spanish language, defining Christianophobia as an “aversion towards Christianity, Christians or anything Christian.”

The word Islamophobia is already in the dictionary alongside antisemitism. 

The Spanish Association of Christian Lawyers, a group that began campaigning for the inclusion of the word in January this year, celebrated the news.

In a statement sent to Crux Now, Polonia Castellanos, president of the group, called it a “historic victory.”

“For us, this is a historic victory, not only for Spanish Christians but for all Spanish speakers. For far too long, hostility and attacks against Christians have been ignored or treated as a minor issue,” she said.

“We found it incomprehensible that the dictionary recognized terms such as Islamophobia and antisemitism, yet did not include a word that explicitly identifies hostility towards Christianity,” she added.

She explained that the organization’s campaign gathered 15,000 signatures in support, and that they formally requested that the RAE include the word in January this year.

“We have always maintained that what cannot be named is much harder to recognize and combat,” Castellanos said.

“The inclusion of Christianophobia will not put an end to attacks against Christians, but it represents a very important step towards raising awareness of this reality and demanding that it receive the same attention…
items.t: ‘Christianophobia’ added to dictionary by Royal Spanish Academy

items.title: Pope Leo returns to what is expected to be a national party in his second homeland of Peru
items.summary:
LIMA, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV arrived in his second homeland of Peru on Wednesday, returning to the place that he credits with teaching him how to be a pastor and where a nationwide party awaits to welcome their beloved “Padre Robert” home.

The visit to Peru marks the final leg of Leo’s three-nation South America tour and its emotional highlight, given the more than two decades that the former Robert Prevost spent in Peru as a missionary priest and later bishop. As a dual citizen of the United States and Peru, he’s the first pope from each country.

Leo’s charter plane touched down at a Lima-area air base, where he was being welcomed by President Keiko Fujimori.

The visit to Peru marks the final leg of Leo’s three-nation South America tour and its emotional highlight, given the more than two decades that the former Robert Prevost spent in Peru as a missionary priest and later bishop. As a dual citizen of the United States and Peru, he’s the first pope from each country.

“My heart is so excited that it makes me want to cry with joy,” said Zuly Castillo, who served as Leo’s secretary when he was bishop of the northern city of Chiclayo near the Pacific Coast. Across from her office, a life-size cardboard cutout of the pope now welcomes visitors to his former residence.

“Peru is the crown of the trip, the homecoming of the first Peruvian pope, no matter where he was born,” said Gustavo Morello, an associate professor of sociology at Boston College and the author of “Lived Religion in Latin America.”

“This is a return to his origins without any doubt,” Morello said.

items.title: The pope ends an emotional Argentina visit with a plea for unity and reconciliation
items.summary:
LUJÁN, Argentina (AP) — Pope Leo XIV closed an emotional and politically charged visit to Argentina on Wednesday with an appeal for unity and reconciliation, offering a parting message of hope to his predecessor’s polarized homeland.

Leo spent his final morning in Argentina ministering to inmates at a prison where the 1976-1983 military junta held political prisoners and covered up a massacre, before celebrating Mass at the national shrine, the Basilica of Our Lady of Luján. 

The Vatican estimated that around 2 million people turned out for the Mass, the latest of the record-setting crowds who have welcomed Leo on the first papal visit to Argentina in nearly four decades.

After subtly pushing back against President Javier Milei’s austerity agenda for three days — defending the dignity of disabled people, the rights of workers and the church’s social justice teaching — Leo offered final words of consolation and peace.

“We are likewise called to receive God’s grace and to undergo processes of forgiveness and reconciliation that renew peace, hope and charity within us,” Leo told pilgrims at the Luján liturgy.

Leo closed his homily by echoing the apostle Peter’s words to a man disabled from birth, recasting the biblical miracle as a call to a battered nation: “Argentina, rise up and walk!”

Wearing vestments in the blue and white of the Argentine flag, Leo prayed to the Virgin of Luján to help Argentines “build bridges of charity and networks of solidarity” and to “inspire in them the desire to continue along paths of reconciliation, communion and mission.”

On November 9, Leo visited the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione in Claypole, a residential facility for more than 400 people with disabilities in the southern Buenos Aires province. items.title: Why Catalans call the rainbow “St. Martin’s arc”
items.summary:
In Catalan, the rainbow is l’arc de Sant Martí — St. Martin’s arc. The name is so embedded in everyday speech that most Catalans use it without wondering where it came from. The reason for such a name, it turns out, involves a freezing beggar, a sudden burst of sunshine, and a legendary contest between the saint and the devil. The better-known legend ties the rainbow directly to the most famous episode in Martin of Tours’ life. Martin, tradition claims, was a Roman soldier stationed in Amiens when, one winter, he encountered a beggar shaking with cold at the city gates. He drew his sword, cut his military cloak in two, and gave half to the man. That night, according to his hagiographer Sulpicius Severus, he dreamed of Christ wearing the half-cloak and saying: “What you did for the least of my brothers, you did for me.” The Catalan version of the legend adds a Read More…

items.title: How a $7 Million CRS Project Changed the Odds for 21,000 Central Africans
items.summary:
When the Catholic Relief Services launched its “I Londo I Mai” (ILIM) project in June 2023, nearly 70 percent of households in three war-scarred towns in the Central African Republic could put an adequate meal on the table.

By the time the $7 million project, which in Sango means “rise up and grow,” ended in May 2025, that figure had dropped to less than 2 percent. Project manager Sean Gallagher told Crux Now that the project supplied households with 1,500 metric tons of food, stocked 1,000 households with goats, sheep, and pigs, and trained 1,000 young entrepreneurs.

He said the project’s success story proves that money put to good use can still have a significant impact on people’s lives. But with humanitarian aid shrinking as funding agencies pull back, Galagher said CRS is casting a wider net to find new funding partners.

“We are continuing to work with the U.S. government as a partner, but we are also actively expanding our funding base, that includes looking for new partners, like the World Bank and the Green Climate Fund, among others,” he told Crux Now .

Following are excerpts of that interview…

Crux Now : What does “I Londo I Mai” mean, and why did you choose a phrase in Sango for the project’s name? 

Gallagher: The name means “rise up and grow.” In Sango, CAR’s national language, it captures ILIM’s purpose: helping families impacted by conflict have enough to eat, while at the same time working to rebuild their jobs and strengthen their ability to bounce back when another crisis hits. Using Sango helps local communities understand the project’s mission and…

items.title: Pope will wrap up Argentina tour with a visit to a prison and a shrine before heading home to Peru
items.summary:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina — Pope Leo XIV will wrap up his visit to Argentina with two poignant moments on Wednesday — a meeting with inmates at a prison with a history linked to the country’s military dictatorship, and a final Mass at Argentina’s national shrine.

Both sites have important sentimental connections to Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis. But Leo’s final Argentine stops will pale in comparison to the emotional highlight of his South American trip, when he returns home later Wednesday to Peru.

A massive national party is planned to greet Leo, who spent over two decades as a missionary priest and bishop in Peru. He is known to Peruvians as Padre Robert and is beloved for ministering to poor communities, especially in times of crisis.

A meeting with inmates as Francis did 

In Buenos Aires, Leo was scheduled to visit the Devoto Prison, where Francis often ministered when he was archbishop of Buenos Aires. Francis celebrated Masses, visited cellblocks housing inmates with AIDS and washed the feet of prisoners during the annual Holy Week ritual.

The prison, inaugurated in 1927, is currently undergoing its definitive closure and transfer of its more than 1,000 inmates to a new penitentiary complex.

During the last military dictatorship (1976–1983), it functioned as a clandestine detention and torture center and was designated as a Memory Site in 2012, to ensure the military repression is not forgotten.
